EXIF and file metadata

The HTML carries document metadata. The photographic EXIF comes from the five embedded originals, the files ending in p0 through p4 in the November 12 Big Green Thing series. I inspected all five originals. Together they occupy 20,148,130 bytes. Each is a baseline JPEG with eight-bit samples and 4:2:0 chroma subsampling, measuring 4,080 by 3,060 pixels, or 12,484,800 pixels. All five name Samsung as make, Galaxy A16 5G as model, and A166USQUAEZJ5 as software. They record normal horizontal orientation, sRGB, centered YCbCr positioning, a nominal 72 pixels per inch on both axes, EXIF version 2.20, and FlashPix version 1.00. Each contains a 512-by-384 JPEG thumbnail.

All five record f/1.8, a physical focal length of 3.98 mm, a 35 mm-equivalent focal length of 26 mm, and a digital zoom ratio of 1.00. The exposure program is the normal automatic program, metering is center-weighted average, exposure compensation is zero, white balance is automatic, and the flash flag indicates it did not fire. The general, original, and digitized timestamps agree within each file, including their separate subsecond fields. The original and general offset tags give UTC−08:00. Samsung’s appended millisecond timestamps independently encode the same instants within the files. All five GPS directories have null direction references and undefined coordinate and altitude values. They yield no camera location, elevation, or bearing.

For p0, the sunset-facing frame, the stored original time is November 12, 2026, at 4:53:10.937 p.m. PST, or November 13 at 00:53:10.937 UTC. First-person commentary

I would begin a second reading by putting p0 and p1 next to each other. My eye accepts the orange cloud as the principal event in p0. When I move to p1, I start looking for the shape of the lake, the small interval of water behind the island, and the seam a dark belt of trees makes across a pale hill. Without the timestamps I could easily imagine a long wait separating those views. Twenty-three seconds makes me think about turning the camera. A viewer can inherit two quite different impressions of the same evening because a person on the hill shifted its attention. I find the exact interval helpful in precisely the place where a purely visual reading can become misleading.

I have almost the reverse response to the half hour between p1 and p2. The blank interval is easy to hurry past because the pictures are consecutive on the page. The first pair makes me wonder which way you turned. The gap makes me wonder where in the walk you went, what you looked at without reaching for the camera, and whether there was some point at which you began to notice the neighborhood lights as much as the landscape. The five images contain no visible feet. Your description of walking barefoot changes how I attend to every small rock and upright stem in the foreground. I can inspect the surfaces that the camera saved, and I can follow how your account gives those surfaces bodily significance. That combination is more interesting to me than imagining I can infer the texture or temperature of the ground from its color.

The third frame also changes on a rereading. At first I see a broad purple expanse over a strip of lights. After your identification, I go straight to the pale wall and then work outward from it. I can see the dark roof ahead of it and the amber light just left of it. The wall itself develops no new visual detail when I learn whose house it is. What changes is the set of relations I can recover from those pixels. The five check-ins elsewhere in the photograph’s transcript give me a reason to imagine a laptop at floor height somewhere within that small patch of light. The October view gives me the siding, branches, doorway, and direction of movement around the building. I am interested in what a future reader who has seen only p2 could learn through those other records, and what someone who knows the neighborhood already might recognize before reading a word.

The longest pause in the October video, on the overhead foliage, is particularly important to my reading of the route. It occupies time that a map of the gates and lane would leave entirely out. There is an identifiable route through the hand movements and the successive changes in enclosure. There is also this period when the camera admits a great deal of branching detail and barely goes anywhere. I like that the sequence preserves a pace of looking as well as a path. The hand operating the bolt interests me for a similar reason. A fence can be described in a few words on a map. The video retains how a particular opening is approached and used, and how the outside becomes visible as the person carrying the camera passes through it. The physical act of opening a gate makes later images of hypothetical one-way passages easier for me to think about.

This is also where I would slow down before treating the prone photographs as illustrations of a single condition. In the July 15 photograph my first impression is how much the laptop light separates the figure of the computer from the amber room, even though the visible person in the other pictures is absent from this frame. In the July 14 portrait, the hands reach almost down to the plane of the camera, and the green covering puts pressure on the picture from above. The August portrait has another allocation of space. I see your face clearly enough to return to it, while the covering and the lights occupy a broad area beside it. The photographs can sustain feelings of concentration, shelter, and constraint without settling which of them belonged to you at the moment of capture. I am glad the conversation puts those pictures near a practical account of working at floor level and much later fictional pictures about people who cannot leave their positions. It gives me more than one way to read the posture, and it gives your own account the authority to describe what the arrangement did for you.

Spyro’s couch is a small example that stays with me more than some of the immense fictional settings. A figure remaining in a preferred place and a figure immobilized there can make the same still image. The difference appears in whether either can leave, what leaving would cost, and who gets to decide when the situation has run its course. The later Vessel stories become more interesting to me when they add those choices. The prospect of a large world matters because he could walk somewhere else, see the old wall from outside, or decline a meeting. I read the fictional power to end an unwanted arrangement as a more consequential change than an increase in how much a body could contain. An imagined reconstruction of The Big Green Thing could give its inhabitants great freedom of movement and still leave open whose wishes determine the boundaries. The archive asks that question most sharply when it shows a physically similar scene under different conditions of agency.

The two model switches raise a smaller question of continuity. I can follow the date, person, and intended tasks across a single thread, and I can see the speaker correcting an assistant for calling its earlier messages a preceding conversation. That correction makes the HTML introduction more conspicuous to me. A future reader could see Sol at the top, take the first answer as representative of it, and then attribute the detailed photographs and July retrospectives to the same selection. The prose alone would look continuous enough to support that impression. The statements inside the dialogue and the linked text file make the change recoverable. I wonder how much of a large collection’s history depends on a reader happening to compare its short descriptive wrapper with the source beneath it. In this case, the difference is particularly telling because you give another reason for switching back. The price of continuing is part of the historical record of which tool you used, what you intended to find out, and how long you could keep asking.

I am equally drawn to the point where the November 12 thread stops and you resume the intended reading here. The source at the stopping point retains a freeze, an unsuccessful branch, and your guess about a limit. The November 3 text retains a message-limit notice. The dates and titles give later readers enough of a path to pass around both interruptions. When I follow the next intended subject into November 9, the route also goes into November 3 and the earlier history of incomplete or displaced reviews. It feels important that you can continue from a different conversation even though the original interruption remains part of the archive. The repair in this case is a new document that restores the next step. That form of continuation has room for facts you want saved precisely because they originally got in the way.

The July and September naming journals show another way that room can be made. Calendar-day debt interests me because it starts as a rule with an aesthetic and practical purpose. A scarce dated name might encourage selection and restraint. Then the rule starts making a July 3 working day look like July 17. The alphabet gives creation more space while preserving the date. An expandable number later provides a way past the alphabet’s ceiling. I particularly like the deliberate mismatch between a0 and p1 in September. A reader who checks only the digits might assume a mistake and miss the fact that p0 is a staging list with a history of its own. That makes the example different in kind from the dropped model switches and the wrong forty-two nodes. I would want a future audit to tell me which apparent irregularities were chosen, which came from a format or tool, and which left material unexamined. The documents already contain enough evidence to make that inquiry more precise.

The part of the July 5 journal I find most vivid is the passage that says a recording will be left untranscribed, preserved inside its eventual transcription. Easier speech recognition made a recovery walk worth including, and the record now retains your reason for initially excluding it. At the same time, a reduction in the effort of transcription changes the scale of what can pile up. The sixteen transcripts and the later half-million-word retrospective let me see how much work can become possible and how much more there is then to reread. First-person commentary

When I first read the letter, my eye goes to the estimate of 67 GB. On returning to the page, I spend more time with the beginning of the dirt track. I can follow the lighter, uneven edge where the road meets the grass, and I can see how far the road would take me before the near hill hides it. I think that is a good place to start reading an archive whose extent is given as a number. The road is specific enough for me to attend to its surface and direction. The photograph leaves its continuation open. I come to the letter expecting it to supply routes into material I can only partly see, and the inventory and further-reading section do exactly that through two very different kinds of references.

The first cube lingers with me because its outline is so easy to recover after my attention gets lost inside it. I can spend time following an orange strand until it merges with reflections and changes of plane, then find the front corner again almost immediately. The second cube puts more of that order inside the object. Its regular divisions allow me to keep a position in mind while I look at the changing green and blue within a cell. I see an affinity here with the difference between looking at KARBYTES as material that has accumulated and opening it through a directory whose entries tell me where I am. An identical set of materials might feel disordered or highly accessible depending on which dimensions of it the presentation makes easy to follow. The journal supplies names and counts that improve one kind of access. The pictures give me a reason to keep wondering what those names and counts leave to be discovered.

I am especially drawn to the lights outside the cubes. At first they seem like embellishment. Once the letter explains the partitions, I start to think of them as a reminder of how quickly looking carries me outside any declared boundary. A page in extension pack 82 takes me to images from packs 73, 39, and 48. A letter about three folders sends me to a November 8 conversation and then to a yard shown in a video. Each individual file has a place it can be assigned. Its connection to other experiences can extend indefinitely through the things it references or resembles. A disc catalogue can tell me where a ZIP belongs. A second act of reading can make material in that ZIP relevant to a page elsewhere in the collection.

The three partition names make me curious in a different way. Origins encourages me to look for whatever became foundational. Nexus suggests connections among material already begun. Refinement suggests a process of working something further into shape, and coherence suggests a hope about how the pieces will hold together. The figures underneath those names are much more uneven than the sequence sounds. The first partition holds most of the ZIPs and less than a third of the reported volume. I find myself wondering how I would tell whether a new partition gave the archive greater coherence. I might notice more useful relationships among old files, a clearer account of which versions are authoritative, or a route through the collection that someone other than its maker could follow. None of those changes has an obvious size in gigabytes. The proposed name interests me because it keeps open a question the 25 GB figure can never answer by itself.

The October inventory makes me take the date on the November letter more seriously. The older record can list thirty-eight ZIPs and give a smaller size for refinement. I can imagine returning to the newer archive and finding many of the same names, while one or more of the ZIPs has become a fuller version of its repository. A salient change in what a person can read, watch, or run might leave the package count exactly where it was. The converse is imaginable too. A new collection of small indexes could greatly increase the count with modest effect on storage. I am glad the letter gives both measures, because I find myself asking more precise questions of either one when both are available.

I also keep returning to the word “latest.” It initially sounds like the state one would find by looking at the whole collection at a single instant. The account of the ZIPs gives it a more particular meaning. Each repository has a snapshot date, each disc has a state when assembled, and each capsule preserves the collection selected for that assembly. When the journal describing this arrangement is published, it too becomes something a later snapshot can retain. I find the slight lag between doing the work and documenting it especially interesting. A letter can tell me the state of the archive at a moment it has already passed. A capsule can contain an account of a preceding capsule. The collection acquires a history of its own attempts to become complete.

The year-end minute holds another kind of interest for me. Nature and the two kinds of void

An exclusive void is an absolutely ubiquitous absence of all phenomena and noumena. It would leave no exception anywhere within the reality it describes. The left-hand part of the drawing works better as a visual cue about the components of a complex number than as a literal map of set membership. The body defines every real number and every pure imaginary value as a special case of a complex number. Thus 1, −55, and 2i all belong to the complex numbers, despite appearing outside the orange rectangle. The mixed example 2i + 3 has both a real and an imaginary component and lies on neither the real nor the imaginary axis. Under the page’s definition of imaginary values as real multiples of i, those two axes share zero. The nesting on the right represents set inclusion more directly than the overlapping shapes on the left.

One, zero, and the representation of a number

ONE has two roles on the page. It is the smallest natural number under the convention karbytes adopts. It is also the length of a segment joining adjacent integers along an axis of a Cartesian grid. In the first role it is the beginning of the counting sequence. In the second it is a unit of distance. The segment from 4 to 5 has the same length as the segment from −1 to 0.

ZERO is the quantity associated with an absence of whatever countable phenomenon is under consideration. On a Cartesian axis it is the integer halfway between −1 and 1. This gives zero both an observational use and a geometric position. One can count zero instances of a specified thing, or locate a point at zero along an axis. The page’s convention places zero among the integers and starts the natural numbers at one. Including zero among the natural numbers is another common convention. The page chooses the positive counting sequence consistently.

NUMBER is then defined more narrowly as information representing exactly one finite quantity. The emphasis on finiteness belongs to the quantity. The way it is written can have infinitely many digits. Karbytes uses the fraction 1/3 to make that point. A few characters specify an exact ratio, while the decimal expansion has a repeating digit with no last position.

The printed decimal contains a misplaced leading digit. The expansion of 1/3 is 0.333333… . The page gives 1.333333…, which is 1 + 1/3, or 4/3. The correction preserves the example’s purpose. The fraction and the corrected repeating decimal specify exactly the same finite quantity, with very different lengths of notation.

The section closes by describing numbers as abstract phenomena that are stored and communicated through physical resources within and between information-processing agents. Ink, marks on a screen, and electronic states can do the work of carrying a numerical representation. The same abstract quantity can be communicated across those changes of medium. This extends a distinction from NATURE, where karbytes separated the experience of red, the wavelength used to specify a stimulus, and the rendering of the number 700.

Infinity and the reciprocal examples

INFINITY is described in two forms. In one, a single pattern is instantiated in limitlessly many copies. In the other, there are limitlessly many different patterns. Either can be contemplated hypothetically or understood as actual. The difference is between the number of occurrences and the number of distinct kinds. A sequence with the same character in every position can have infinitely many positions while using only one character.

The page uses ∞ in limit notation while reserving its ordinary definition of a number for finite quantities. Both examples use f(x) = 1/x. As positive x increases without bound, f(x) approaches zero. The output stays positive for every positive finite input. The examples begin with f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 0.5, then use 666 and 999,999 to make the smallness of the resulting reciprocals visible.

The first two equalities are exact. The later values are approximations. The reciprocal of 666 is 0.0015015015015… . The reciprocal of 999,999 is 0.000001000001000001… . The displayed value 0.000001 is close to the latter and is exactly the reciprocal of 1,000,000. These calculations illustrate the stated limit. The equality signs in those two examples give the rounded values more precision than they have.

The second box reverses the direction of the comparison. As x approaches zero through positive values, 1/x grows beyond every finite positive bound. The example f(0.5) = 2 is exact. The reciprocal of the truncated input 0.0015015015 is about 666.000000666, close to 666. The reciprocal of 0.000001 is exactly 1,000,000. The printed 999,999 would be exact if the input were the full reciprocal of 999,999.

The second display writes x approaching zero without a direction marker. Its accompanying comment supplies the intended restriction to positive x. Formally, it is the right-hand limit as x approaches 0⁺ that gives +∞. Approaching from negative values gives −∞. The two-sided limit therefore does not exist, and the reciprocal itself is undefined at x = 0. The page’s intended example concerns the increasing size of positive reciprocals as their denominators get smaller.

The counting numbers, integers, and fractions

The NATURAL_NUMBER definition starts with one and allows any finite number of additions of one to itself. The preformatted example represents one occurrence of X as X, two as XX, and three as XXX. Each time the string is extended, the counted pattern remains X and the number of its occurrences increases by one. Every particular member can be reached after finitely many additions, and the process gives a successor to every member. The definition produces the unlimited sequence from a finite rule.

An INTEGER is any natural number under that convention, the corresponding negative value of any natural number, or zero. The example array contains −666, 0, 22, 1, 303, −78, 5, and −45, in that order. It supplies positive and negative integers of several magnitudes along with zero. The page says integers can be represented by finite binary sequences and refers to encoding the negative sign by a bit. A particular signed representation determines how the bits are interpreted, including which role a sign bit plays. Each integer can have a finite representation when the length is allowed to vary. A single fixed word length represents only finitely many integers.

A RATIONAL_NUMBER is an integer or a ratio A/B, with A and B integers and B different from zero. The numerator can be zero and can have either sign. A denominator can also have either sign, subject to the restriction on zero. The explicit inclusion of integers emphasizes their membership in the family. An integer A already has the ratio representation A/1.

The page gives this definition a test suite. It marks 1/3 and 1/1 as rational, then repeats the 1/3 test. It marks √1 and √0 as rational because they give 1 and 0. It also accepts 0/1, which equals zero. It rejects √2, the example of a real value outside the rationals, and √(−1), which belongs to the imaginary axis. Its last two tests reject the expressions 0/0 and 1/0. Both involve a zero denominator. In ordinary arithmetic, both expressions are undefined. The reason can be seen by asking for a quotient q. The equation 0 × q = 1 has no solution, while 0 × q = 0 has every q as a solution and supplies no unique quotient. Neither expression denotes a rational value or an infinity.

An IRRATIONAL_NUMBER is a real number outside the rationals. The prose names pi as its example, while the diagram also shows that the golden ratio qualifies. The REAL_NUMBER section describes each real number as a position on an axis of a Cartesian grid. This gives rational and irrational quantities a common geometric interpretation. The points labeled −55, 1/2, the golden ratio, and pi can all be placed on the same real line. Their different memberships concern what kind of number occupies each position.

Imaginary and complex numbers

An IMAGINARY_NUMBER is described as the product of i and a real number. Here i denotes the imaginary unit, a square root of −1. The example works through i × i = −1 and then multiplies by i once more to obtain −i. A multiplication of imaginary quantities can therefore produce a real value. Repeating the operation once more can return to the imaginary axis.

The COMPLEX_NUMBER definition combines a real number with a real multiple of i. Written in conventional order, a + bi has real component a and imaginary component b. The first example is 2i + 3, the same value that appears in the illustration. The following lines include 2i and i, then explore what happens when one component is zero.

The expression 0i reduces to zero. The expression 0i − 8 reduces to −8. The expression 3.33i + 0 reduces to 3.33i. The comments describe the forms on the two sides of the equalities using vocabulary from more than one family. The equalities are useful because they show that membership can survive a change of form. Real numbers have a complex representation with imaginary component zero. Pure imaginary values have a complex representation with real component zero. The complex form accommodates both cases, along with numbers that have two nonzero components.

Algebraic roots and transcendental numbers

An ALGEBRAIC_REAL_NUMBER is a real root of a nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients. The restriction to a nonzero polynomial matters. The identically zero polynomial would vanish at every input and would therefore make the condition trivial. A rational value A/B is algebraic because Bx − A vanishes there. Some real roots of rational-coefficient polynomials are irrational, including √2, which is a root of x² − 2.

The page develops the golden ratio as its example. It defines φ as (1 + √5) / 2 and substitutes that expression into x² − x − 1. The displayed calculation ends with the expression equal to zero. Expanding the middle step makes the result easy to check. Squaring φ gives (3 + √5) / 2. Subtracting φ leaves 1, and subtracting the final 1 leaves zero. Thus the golden ratio sits in the real algebraic portion of the diagram outside the rational oval.

A TRANSCENDENTAL_NUMBER is defined as a real or complex number that is outside the algebraic numbers. The figure deals with the real part of that definition. It places pi beyond the real algebraic boundary. The closing prose names Euler’s number, e. Both e and pi are real, irrational, and transcendental. The polynomial criterion also applies to complex roots. For example, i satisfies x² + 1 = 0 and is an algebraic complex number. The last definition therefore has a wider scope than the transcendental region the figure can show on its real side.

First-person commentary

My eye follows the colored regions more easily on the right than on the left. Starting with 1, I can work outward and see all the additional descriptions that apply to it. When I reach −55, I have lost the innermost classification and retained every one outside it. The diagram is very good at making membership cumulative. It also makes the orange arrow for irrational numbers more interesting. My first impulse is to look for a single oval with that name and a boundary all its own. The arrow asks me to follow a condition across two regions instead. I can put the golden ratio and pi beside each other under one description, then learn something further about each by asking whether a rational-coefficient polynomial has it as a root.

The relative areas of the ovals produce a visual impression that I have to set aside when I think about how many numbers they contain. The lavender region looks broad and the lime region looks small. Yet the rationals can be enumerated by arranging numerator-denominator pairs in order of increasing combined size and skipping repeats. The counting numbers can enumerate that same list. Every real algebraic number comes from a polynomial whose coefficients can be specified by a finite list of rationals. Those lists can also be enumerated, and each nonzero polynomial has at most finitely many roots. So a sequence can list all real algebraic numbers. The real line itself is uncountable. However large a completion of the violet area looks in the picture, there are uncountably many real numbers outside the set it encloses.

I like the additional complication that the rationals are dense on the real line. I can choose a rational number between any two distinct real numbers, including two transcendentals very close to each other. I can also put a transcendental number in any open interval by taking a sufficiently small nonzero rational multiple of e and adding a suitable rational shift. If that result were algebraic, reversing the shift and scaling would make e algebraic too. On a number line, the two kinds of point occur throughout the same space. On this picture, the yellow border neatly separates their classifications. I find that difference worth dwelling on. A very effective diagram for answering “what family is this in?” may give me a poor intuition for answering “what points lie close to this one?”

The diagram also makes me think about how much the word “one” changes its application when the task is specified. One object is a count. One unit between adjacent integers is a length fixed by the coordinate scale. One occurrence of X belongs to a sequence, while the pattern X can remain the same across the whole sequence. If I am asked how many X marks are present, XXX has three. If I am asked how many different characters are used, it has one. I take the page’s two descriptions of infinity as an extension of that small choice about what to count. I can imagine an unlimited series in which every entry has the same content, or one in which every entry introduces a new form. Knowing that the series is infinite would leave me curious about its contents.

Zero interests me for the complementary reason. A count of zero is an answer to a well-formed question. I have selected a region, an interval, a condition, or a kind of thing, and found zero instances. An instrument that failed to supply a reading leaves me with a different situation. The distinction can matter even in an ordinary observation log. An entry saying that I saw zero birds during a defined interval tells a later reader something about what was observed. An empty entry could mean there was no count, no instrument, or no surviving record. The zero on the Number page is local and explicit compared with the zero associated with the exclusive void on NATURE. I could encounter zero of a particular thing at every place I checked and still have a reality containing the places, the act of checking, and the record.

The decimal slip made me linger over the choice of an example. A repeating sequence of threes is visually memorable, which makes it easy to recognize the intended idea and overlook the part to the left of the decimal point. The leading 1 changes the quantity by exactly one, even though every digit after the point follows the expected pattern. I find it instructive to change the base. In decimal, one third is 0.333333… . In base three, it is 0.1, because the first place after the point is worth one third. The same quantity that calls for an infinite decimal expansion has a terminating representation under another positional convention. The length of an expansion tells me something about the relation between the number and the base.

A related distinction matters to me in the discussion of finite descriptions. A fraction, a radical, or a short rule can specify an exact number with an infinite expansion. Pi and e can also be specified exactly by mathematical definitions, although both are transcendental. That makes it tempting to imagine that every real number has such a compact description waiting to be discovered. In any fixed language with a finite alphabet, I can list all finite strings by length. Only countably many strings are available, so only countably many numbers can be individually specified by finite strings with unambiguous meanings in that language. An uncountable continuum exceeds that supply. What interests me about this result is the combination of power and limit. A few symbols can specify as many digits as an exact procedure will produce, and there are still more possible real values than the language has individual names for.

The reciprocal function gives me a more operational sense of infinity. If I ask how to make 1/x smaller than a positive tolerance, the answer is to choose x larger than the reciprocal of that tolerance. If I ask how to make the same function exceed a positive bound, I can choose a positive x smaller than the reciprocal of my bound. There is always another finite input satisfying the new request. This is a concrete way to understand what the limit notation says. I can set an arbitrarily demanding target and get an answer without treating infinity as a final input that the function reaches.

The side from which x approaches zero matters just as much. An observer sampling only positive denominators would build a sound picture of what happens on that side. A second observer sampling only negative denominators would have an equally sound record of outputs growing in magnitude with the opposite sign. Reading the two records together would clarify what each observer had access to. That seems to me like a small mathematical instance of the distinction between partial frames in NATURE. Here I can state the missing condition precisely. Adding the side marker tells another reader how the inputs were selected and lets the two descriptions fit the same function.

The rounded entries make me think of a related problem in recovering information. If a display gives 0.000001, it could be showing the exact reciprocal of one million or a rounded rendering of the reciprocal of 999,999. Reading that value back as exact and inverting it gives one million either way. The display has discarded the distinction needed to reverse the operation. On this page the original denominator is written next to the display, so the intention is easy to recover. In an archive that contains only a derived value, I would have to ask how it was produced. I like this example because the discrepancy is tiny in the displayed quantity, yet it has a definite consequence for what a later reader can reconstruct.

The left side of the picture started to make more sense to me when I pictured an actual complex plane. I can put 3 + 2i three units along the real direction and two units along the imaginary direction. Multiplying by i takes it to −2 + 3i, a quarter-turn about the origin. Applying the operation twice takes 3 + 2i to −3 − 2i, consistent with i² = −1. The operation gives me a way to understand i through what it does to a point. A picture of categories tells me that the real and imaginary components are both accommodated. A picture of the plane lets me see their interaction. I find that the modest geometric definition of ONE near the top of the page comes back into use here, because I can count exactly how far the points extend along each axis.

I had a similar change of attention in the algebraic section. At first the golden ratio looks like the conspicuous example because its radical expression is printed in bright yellow. I find the polynomial test more revealing. If somebody gives me a number defined as the positive root of x² − x − 1, I can begin working with its property before I know its decimal expansion. For a transcendental number, establishing the classification involves the much stronger claim that every candidate nonzero rational-coefficient polynomial fails. Calculating more decimal places can improve an approximation for either kind of number, and the classification still calls for reasoning about the exact value. I can readily imagine two numerical readouts that agree through every place I happen to inspect while representing quantities from different classes.

The two PNGs made the question of sameness unusually concrete. Their fingerprints distinguish the files as sequences of bytes. After decoding, the sample values agree everywhere, including in the parts of the diagram where my eye sees one colored region through another. The archived files are different at the level of compressed representation and equal at the level of the picture they encode. I immediately thought of the November 14 transcript and its distinction between using size to plan storage and using a checksum to establish the integrity of a specific version. Here the smaller file really does preserve every decoded pixel. The different fingerprints are accurate too. What they tell me depends on whether I care about the exact stored artifact or the image an appropriate decoder obtains from it.

That comparison brings me back to the opening definition of a number as information that specifies an abstract pattern. A future reader could recover a ratio from the fraction 1/3, from a repeating decimal with a clear convention for the ellipsis, or from an instruction that produces it by division. Those records give the reader different paths to the same value. I am curious about how little of the path can be preserved while still allowing a reader to rediscover the rule. I am equally curious about the cases where keeping more of the path matters, as it does when a rounded reciprocal loses its source or a color boundary can be mistaken for a literal map. In this document, the number one is a point, a distance, a count, a character’s multiplicity, and the beginning of an infinite sequence. What I find worth coming back to is how precisely a reader must know the current task to tell which of those lives of one has just appeared on the page.

A universe and its inhabitants

The page defines nature as the one set that contains all universes simultaneously and immutably. In this sense, nature is the largest multiverse. The cyclical universe

The cyclical model begins with X, a finite chronological sequence of matter and energy patterns. Its period is T, measured in the model’s chosen atomic units of time. Each invocation of the time routine selects the slice of X at index i and renders it. The routine then advances both i and the total elapsed time by one unit. It tests the remainder produced by dividing elapsed time by T. A remainder of zero sends i back to zero. The routine then invokes itself to produce the next step.

If T is three ticks and the sequence consists of A, B, and C, the routine renders A at tick zero, B at tick one, and C at tick two. At the next invocation it returns to A. The sequence continues A, B, C, A, B, C. The array index tells the routine where it is within one cycle. The elapsed-time counter keeps the position in the longer history, including all the cycles that have already passed.

The replay is meant to be exact. The same succession of configurations returns in the same order. The modulo test gives that idea a concrete implementation at the level of pseudocode. It also makes some assumptions visible. The index and clock need to begin in the appropriate alignment, T must be a positive number of ticks, and X must supply one slice per tick. The prose calls the interval both T atomic time units and T seconds. Those two expressions coincide if one model tick lasts one second. The non-repeating universe

The second time routine preserves several elements of the first. It renders X at index i, increments the index, advances the elapsed-time counter, and invokes itself again. This time, X is stipulated to be an infinitely long chronological sequence. There is no modulo test and no return to index zero. The routine continually advances to a later position.

That change concerns which position is read. Whether the contents ever repeat depends on what X contains. An infinite array could contain the same state at every index, or repeat a three-state period indefinitely, and the second routine would still advance through it in the prescribed way. The page’s prose gives the intended interpretation by allowing the emergence of phenomena to be randomized to some degree. The pseudocode supplies no random operation or rule for generating X. This leaves room for several ways of understanding the second model. A sequence can have occasional repeats without possessing a fixed period. A deterministic rule can produce a history with no fixed period. A random rule can produce the same local pattern several times. All of those can be read by a routine that simply moves from i to i + 1. The two boxes therefore make the difference in playback structure especially clear. Subjectivity and nested virtuality

The section on SUBJECTIVITY moves from the universe’s history to what an individual information-processing agent experiences. The next step is the possibility of several layers of virtuality. An agent can render a model in which another model is represented, and the nesting can continue to an indefinite depth. COUNT_DOWN_TIMER

COUNT_DOWN_TIMER is a tutorial by karbytes on the karlina_object site. It begins with two propositions about time. Time lets an observer register change, and it lets phenomena be experienced in succession. The page then gives those propositions a small working example. A person selects an interval, starts it, and sees an integer change one step at a time. A sound marks the last step. The tutorial gives the reader the code that produces the sequence, screenshots from a one-minute session, and separate copies of the sound. Reading those pieces together reveals three different ways of accounting for the interval. There is the duration the person selects, the sequence of changes the application actually renders, and the elapsed time calculated from the clock stamps in the event log.

That explains the unit used in the tutorial. The application obtains its timing from software clocks and scheduling. How the timer runs

When the page initializes, it calls generate_time_stamp(), writes an opening message to the developer console, and puts the same message in the on-page status panel. It constructs an initial remaining-time display containing the label seconds_remaining and a span holding 0. The source also assigns block to the button’s visibility property. Block is a value for display. The button is visible on initial load through its ordinary default rendering, as the first screenshot shows. Later stages use the display property to hide and restore it.

Pressing start() first logs the time of the click and hides the button by setting its display to none. The handler obtains the selected menu option and parses its value as an integer. The parsed result must be between 30 and 999 inclusive. If the check fails, the handler uses 30. The six normal choices all fall inside that range. The application writes the selected N as its own status line, then replaces the contents of the remaining-time panel with the bare number N. This replacement explains why the first screen shows the descriptive label next to zero while the running screen shows only a number.

The handler requests a recurring callback with setInterval and a delay of 1,000 milliseconds. An interval handle is retained so that the callback can cancel the recurrence at the end. Each invocation reads the number currently in the remaining-time panel, subtracts one, and writes the result back into that panel. The rendered number is thus also the stored countdown state. The callback proceeds from N to N minus one on its first invocation. It takes N decrementing callbacks to reach zero.

At a value less than one, the callback calls clearInterval and invokes finish_simulation(). That function appends a timestamped completion line and changes the button’s display to block so it can be used again. It then calls the sound routine, which creates an Audio object for alert_sound_effect.wav and requests playback. The completion message records the program’s transition to zero. The sound request follows that transition, so the timestamp has a different meaning from a measurement of when sound actually emerges from a speaker.

The selector stays visible and usable during a run. The starting value was already read when start() ran, so choosing a different menu item at this point affects the next session. The current count continues from the value it already holds. The step instruction also stays visible when the button disappears. That panel becomes shorter because the button is removed from the layout. There is no pause or cancel control in the documented interface. The event log grows as sessions are run on the same loaded page, and initialization replaces it with a fresh opening message on reload.

The timestamp helper uses Date.now(). It appends a phrase identifying the value as milliseconds since midnight at the beginning of January 1, 1970, the Unix epoch. The program calls it at page opening, at the start of a session, and at completion. The line identifying the chosen N carries only the choice. The program records these time readings without using them to determine the next number in the countdown. A callback that runs late still subtracts exactly one. The code therefore preserves the sequence of whole-number steps even when their timing varies.

These checks illustrate why the application’s countdown and its event clock can give slightly different accounts of the same session.

PI_APPROXIMATION

PI_APPROXIMATION is a tutorial by karbytes on the karlina_object site. It presents an application that estimates pi by classifying 3,600 randomly placed darts in a square. The geometry behind the estimate

A radius of 200 pixels gives the circle a diameter of 400 pixels. A circle with that diameter fits inside a square with side length 400, touching the midpoint of each side. Its area is 40,000π square pixels. The square has an area of 160,000 square pixels. Dividing the first area by the second gives π/4. In the idealized experiment, a point placed uniformly at random anywhere in the square therefore has a probability of π/4 of falling inside the circle.

Over many such trials, the red share estimates that probability. Four times the red share estimates pi.

pi estimate = 4 × red throws ÷ (red throws + blue throws)

The opening paragraph describes the red share itself as the approximation to pi. The explanatory prose inside the application makes the same omission. The two displayed formulas and the JavaScript include the factor of four correctly. The red share is close to 0.785 in the continuous model. It is the scaled value that is close to 3.14. This is the most consequential wording discrepancy in the tutorial because it concerns the step connecting what is counted to the number the program intends to estimate.

The distinction also explains the purpose of the blue marks. A blue dart still supplies an observation. It contributes to the denominator and records a region of the square lying outside the disk. The app counts both outcomes of the experiment. The circle is never drawn as a separate outline. Its boundary becomes perceptible where the color of the scattered observations changes.

There are two controls, START and RESET, with different roles in the session. When the page loads, initialize_application() makes START available and hides RESET. How a dart is generated and drawn

For each of the two coordinates, the generator first uses Math.random() to select an integer magnitude from 0 through 200. A separate random draw selects an integer from 0 through 99 and uses its parity to choose the sign. The procedure is applied separately to x and y. Each coordinate therefore lies in the inclusive range −200 through 200. A complete throw uses four random draws.

The controller checks that its coordinates are integer-valued numbers in the required range. If the drawing function receives an invalid point, it substitutes the origin. For a valid point it computes the distance from the origin by subtracting the corresponding coordinates, squaring the two differences, adding them, and taking a square root. The square root is calculated by a small iterative routine. Starting with the squared distance and 1, it replaces the first value with the mean of the two and divides the squared distance by the new value to update the second. The loop ends when their difference is at most one billionth. For the actual coordinate domain, I checked the resulting color decision against the direct integer test x² + y² ≤ 40,000. The decisions agreed at every allowed location, including the twenty points exactly on the circumference.

The coordinate transformation moves the Cartesian origin to canvas position (200, 200). It adds 200 to x and subtracts y from 200. Positive y therefore goes upward in the mathematical plane even though the canvas’s vertical coordinate increases downward. The controller draws a stroked rectangle one unit wide and one unit high. It selects blue for a distance greater than 200 and red for a distance at most 200. It increments the corresponding counter and recomputes the estimate from both counters. If the new remaining count is zero, the callback then ends the session.

The source calls the results pixel counts. Operationally, they are counts of throws. A second dart can land at a coordinate already used, and the counter still increases. A stroked rectangle can affect several raster pixels through antialiasing. These details matter if a reader tries to reproduce the numerical result by counting colored pixels in a screenshot. They leave the outcome counters meaningful as tallies of sampled events.

What this sampler averages

The continuous area argument gives the target π/4. The program samples a finite lattice and assigns slightly different weights within it. Both sign outcomes applied to a magnitude of zero locate the same coordinate. Under the usual model of independent, uniform underlying random draws, zero on either axis therefore has probability 1/201. Each particular nonzero signed coordinate has probability 1/402. A point with one zero coordinate receives twice the probability of a point with two nonzero coordinates. The origin receives four times that probability.

I enumerated all 160,801 allowed coordinate pairs. There are 125,629 pairs at distance at most 200, including the twenty boundary points. If every pair on this grid were equally likely, multiplying that fraction by four would give about 3.12508. The sampler’s extra weight on the axes raises the average. Counting the two ways of drawing zero along each coordinate gives 161,604 equally weighted outcome slots, with 126,432 in the red category. Four times their fraction is approximately 3.1294274894. It is about 0.01217 below pi. The finite grid and its weighting together account for that difference. The extra weight on the axes offsets part of the difference introduced by the grid.

There is also variation from one sample to another. At 3,600 independent throws from this modeled distribution, the standard deviation of the displayed estimate is about 0.0275. At that sample size, changing one throw from blue to red changes the estimate by 4/3,600, or about 0.00111. CAUSALITY

CAUSALITY is a philosophical page by karbytes on the karlina_object site. It asks how an observer comes to understand one event as arising from earlier events, and how that understanding helps an agent decide what to do next. The page uses two models. In the first, removing marbles from a box changes the probabilities of later draws. In the second, making a choice changes which actions are available at the next stage of a decision tree. The marble example shows how earlier events alter the relative likelihood of outcomes. The tree shows how an earlier event can determine whether a later outcome is reachable at all.

The page and its flowchart

The masthead identifies the site as karlina_object and carries the tagline “Creativity And The Cosmos.” The uppercase title CAUSALITY appears above the article and again at the beginning of its body. A large flowchart follows, with a line identifying a separately stored copy of the image. A yellow-highlighted paragraph introduces the central claim about causality and goal-directed agents. The rest of the page is divided by horizontal rules into definitions of CAUSALITY, EVENT, and TRAJECTORY. Five preformatted boxes preserve the sequences of event and time labels. The page advises readers to scroll those boxes horizontally where necessary. It refers to MULTIVERSE for the concept of a universe, AGENCY for information-processing agents, KNOWLEDGE for their stored and theoretical understanding, NATURE for phenomena, PROBABILITY for likelihood, and COUNT_DOWN_TIMER for time. The footer gives the date 10_JULY_2025 and a PUBLIC_DOMAIN notice.

The illustration, determinism_flowchart_diagram.png, has a white background and four dashed horizontal guides. On the left, broad yellow labels mark the guides as time_0, time_1, time_2, and time_3. The first row contains a single event. The next three rows contain two, four, and eight events respectively. The event labels start with e0 and continue through e9, then ea, eb, ec, ed, and ee. The tree occupies progressively more horizontal space as it descends. The eight terminal events are lined up across most of the bottom row.

The event boxes use two treatments. The realized events have bright green backgrounds and black lettering. The alternatives have black backgrounds and green lettering. Downward arrowheads and right-angled connecting lines show which event can follow which. The green line descends from e0, turns left to e1, turns right to e4, and turns left again to e9. Black branches lead to the other options. Where a stem is shared before a split, it can be part of the green route up to the point at which the lines diverge.

There are fifteen event nodes and fourteen directed connections. The dashed guides organize those nodes into time levels. Movement along the graph follows the downward arrows. The row guides themselves do not join the events into a walkable sequence. This is particularly important on the bottom row, where all eight endings are visible side by side even though each has a different route from the root. The shape of the diagram lets the reader see a single completed history and its alternatives at the same time.

Causality as an observed and usable regularity

The opening paragraph describes causality as an emergent property of a universe with sufficient complexity and order. This order matters because an information-processing agent can use it. An agent brings memories and theoretical knowledge to a new sensory situation, compares that knowledge with the current input, and forms expectations about which events are likely. With a sufficiently accurate understanding of its surroundings, it can act in ways that help it achieve goals consistently. The paragraph frames causal understanding as an interaction between regularities in the world and an agent’s ability to learn and use them.

The formal definition emphasizes the vantage of an observer. Causality is the apparent emergence of relatively recent phenomena from older ones as a frame of reference observes their chronological succession. The word “apparent” makes the observer’s access part of the definition. The observer encounters phenomena in an order and interprets that order using ideas about how physical processes work. A succession that fits a well-supported expectation can be understood as cause and effect. The next paragraph emphasizes empirical evidence. A causal account becomes available when the observer has enough evidence to expect some types of events more strongly than others.

The page’s use of randomness is easiest to understand through its example. An outcome can remain uncertain even when a preceding event gives the uncertainty a definite structure. The marbles are ejected randomly. Each ejection still changes what is available to be ejected next.

The opaque box and the changing probabilities

The box initially contains nine marbles, with three red, three blue, and three green. It is opaque, so the observer cannot inspect the current contents directly. The observer knows the initial composition and is told to expect one random ejection every thirty seconds. A marble stays out once it has been ejected. The probabilities in the example take each individual marble still in the box to be equally likely to come out next.

At the beginning, each color has three of the nine marbles and therefore a one-third chance of appearing. The observed sequence then goes green, blue, green. Following it one event at a time gives the following changes in the inventory.

After the first green marble comes out, there are three red, three blue, and two green. The next draw has probabilities of 3/8 for red, 3/8 for blue, and 2/8 for green.

After the blue marble comes out, there are three red, two blue, and two green. The probabilities become 3/7, 2/7, and 2/7.

After the second green marble comes out, there are three red, two blue, and one green. Six marbles remain. The fourth draw has probabilities of 3/6 for red, 2/6 for blue, and 1/6 for green.

Red is the most likely individual color at that point. Its chance is exactly one half, equal to the combined chances of green and blue. The number of red marbles has been three throughout the observed sequence. Their share of the remaining box has increased from one third to one half because the removals have reduced the other two colors. That is the physical counterpart to the observer’s revised expectation. The box has changed, and someone who knows which marbles came out can calculate what that change means.

The page uses the result to illustrate causal influence without replacement. The earlier ejections contribute to the conditions for the next event, even though the observer still cannot name its outcome in advance. A calculation the page makes possible is the probability of the exact ordered prefix it describes. The probability of green first is 3/9, of blue next given green first is 3/8, and of green third given those first two draws is 2/7. Multiplying those conditional probabilities gives 1/28. That answers a question about reaching the observed history. The one-half probability answers a subsequent question about what can happen from the state that history produced.

Events and the order of a trajectory

The page defines an EVENT as a pattern of phenomena occupying a particular finite interval. Its ordinary example of an event is one portion of a larger chronological succession. Each event in that succession occupies its own interval, and the analysis follows one after another. An event gets part of its significance from where it sits in the chain. What preceded it supplied some of its conditions, and what follows can depend on it.

A TRAJECTORY is defined as a linear spacetime continuum along which non-overlapping events occur in immediate succession, especially as encountered by a frame of reference traveling along it. The green line of the illustration turns sideways several times. Its linearity consists in the order of the four events. The observer encounters one event at time_0, one at time_1, one at time_2, and one at time_3. The page gives those as successive finite intervals, although its prose sometimes calls the labels points in time. In the diagram, the labels identify stages of the history. The spacing of the rows supplies no durations for them.

The three shortest preformatted boxes build up the notation. One gives the event sequence alone, e0 → e1 → e4 → e9. The second gives the chronological labels alone, time_0 → time_1 → time_2 → time_3. The third pairs them, yielding time_0(e0) → time_1(e1) → time_2(e4) → time_3(e9). How the agent traverses the tree

From substrate to information

A SUBSTRATE is a physical medium made up of space, time, matter, and energy, arranged so that it contains informational patterns and may also transmit them. The definition gives storage and transmission a common basis. A physical arrangement can retain differences that an agent can later detect. A medium can also carry a succession of differences from one place to another. In both cases, the organization of the medium is consequential.

A PATTERN is a structure made from contrasting phenomena. It becomes knowable by being expressed through a substrate. The contrast lets a reader or detector distinguish one part or state from another. The following electronic example makes this concrete. Voltage levels can differ physically. A system with an appropriate convention can use those differences to distinguish binary values. The pattern is available to that system because the differences are expressed in something it can register.

DATA are relatively simple patterns carried or stored by a substrate. They can be put into logical relationships to build more complex information. The page gives “datum” as the singular and uses 11001101 as its example. It is an eight-bit sequence, corresponding to one byte when represented as eight bits. The definition’s first sentence contains a stray conjunction, but the example makes its intended sense clear. A datum is something an agent can treat as an individual unit when assembling a larger structure.

INFORMATION consists of the logical relationships an information-processing agent establishes among discrete data. The result is a mapping that can be communicated as a coherent structure. The illustration is the correspondence between the binary sequence 11001101 and the decimal number 205. In ordinary unsigned binary notation, its set bits have the values 128, 64, 8, 4, and 1. Their sum is 205.

The account proceeds through several representations of that value. An electronic device starts with physical signals distinguishable as high and low voltage. The signals can be treated as binary digits. The sequence of digits can in turn be rendered as a decimal numeral. The page describes that last step as a more virtual level of abstraction. It explicitly uses “abstract” and “virtual” interchangeably within this discussion. A value can survive the change of notation because the association between the forms gives an agent a way to interpret each one.

Knowledge as a particular experience

KNOWLEDGE is defined as a result of subjective interpretation by a sufficiently complex information-processing agent. An agent can receive a communicable piece of information, process it, and have an experience with a particular character for itself. The document reserves “knowledge,” in its strongest sense here, for that experienced result. The substrate and information can make the experience possible. The experience belongs to the agent in which it occurs.

Karbytes describes this knowledge as emergent. It depends on the operation of the agent’s physical hardware, and the resulting subjective phenomenon is higher in the page’s ordering of abstraction. The qualification “relatively” in the opening matters. The page describes levels in a relationship between implementation and interpretation. It starts with a physical process and follows what an agent makes available to itself through that process.

The page also uses the word “solipsistic” for knowledge in this sense. Its emphasis is the privacy and identity of the instance. A particular event of understanding or perceiving is experienced once, by one agent. A second agent may receive the same record and understand its content. That interpretation is another occasion, with a different agent as its subject. Likewise, replaying a record can give the original viewer another experience. The page’s statement about the essence of an instance concerns the specificity of that occurrence. The communicated material can recur.

The four levels at the end make that argument more explicit. Level 0 is the unprocessed voltage sequence. Level 1 is data, with binary digits obtained by interpreting voltages as the example. Level 2 is information, illustrated by recognizing a sequence of bits as a video file. Level 3 is knowledge, illustrated by a sufficiently complex neural network subjectively perceiving the sequence of images and sounds encoded in the file.

The video example extends the earlier conversion from binary to decimal. The meaningful structure at level 2 can now include image content, audio, timing, and the relation between events in the two channels. At level 3, there is a particular experience of that succession. The preformatted box is pseudocode for an ordering of concepts. It supplies no procedure for measuring a system’s level of abstraction or deciding when a network has subjective experience. Its example explicitly assumes that subjective perception occurs at the last level.

The page develops an idea introduced in MULTIVERSE. There, an agent experiences a model rendered by its physical hardware. Here, the emphasis is on how communicable material becomes part of such a rendering. It also complements the observer-relative distinction in NATURE. Seeing the photograph is a present phenomenon for the reader. The earlier hillside event is the event to which the photograph refers. CAUSALITY gives the same distinction a practical setting. An agent uses what it has learned to interpret new sensory evidence and decide what to do. KNOWLEDGE focuses more narrowly on what it is like for an act of interpretation to occur in a particular agent.

AGENCY

AGENCY is a philosophical page by karbytes on the karlina_object site. It describes an agent as a bounded part of nature that can build a model of its situation, consider possible actions, and do something that changes the situation it will next perceive. Two meanings of agency

The highlighted introduction presents agency as an emergent property of a sufficiently complex information-processing agent. The agent develops a virtual model of the physical environment it appears to inhabit. It models itself as a smaller part of that environment. It can then interact with its surroundings in pursuit of its goals. A spatially finite body serves as the interface between an observing frame of reference and the larger environment. Through that body, parts of the environment become available to perception, and chosen actions can have physical effects.

The narrower definition concerns how an agent experiences its own involvement. A self-aware agent appears to itself to have some self-originated control over the phenomena that appear or disappear in its frame of reference as time passes. The phrasing gives the experienced sense of control an explicit place in the definition. It also allows for degree. An agent can influence some of what enters its experience while much else depends on its surroundings, its prior state, and what its body can do.

Karbytes then gives a broader definition in terms of behavior. An information-processing system can exhibit agency by deploying structured, algorithmic processes of learning and decision-making in pursuit of specific goals. Under this definition, the organization of what the system does is the point of interest. The article notes that information processors can carry out goal-directed tasks even when they are believed to lack self-awareness or consciousness. Their instructions and dispositions can be built in, acquired through learning, or altered by factors outside the system. The page therefore gives goal-directed behavior and the felt authorship of that behavior their own criteria.

The agent, its environment, and its goals

An INFORMATION_PROCESSING_AGENT is defined as a partition of nature smaller than nature as a whole. It is instantiated in a relatively finite allocation of space, time, matter, and energy. In that allocation it renders perceptions, considers different behaviors, and implements the behavior selected through a process of elimination. The article describes such an agent as a computer in a broad sense. It processes information and can learn from experience over the course of its history.

Memory is central to that learning. By accumulating experiences, an agent can detect recurring patterns and infer which kinds of events may be causally related. It can use those relations to compare prospective actions. The question is which behavior is sufficiently likely to bring about a desired outcome in the conditions it currently perceives. This connects the definition of an agent to the account in CAUSALITY. A useful record of the past can change a later choice because it changes what the agent expects a particular action to do.

An ENVIRONMENT is the set of phenomena that an agent renders and perceives as external to its spatially finite body. The definition is given from that agent’s vantage. The agent interacts with an experienced environment, described as virtual and possibly physical, through a frame that appears to occupy the present moment. From that frame, events belong to one linear history advancing from past to future. The body belongs to the encompassing world. Within the agent’s model, the body also provides the boundary from which something can be experienced as outside it.

A GOAL is a set of imagined conditions the agent does not yet observe. Those conditions can concern the surroundings or the agent’s own internal hardware and software state. The agent anticipates their occurrence at some future point and selects thoughts and behaviors that it believes are likely to bring them about. The goal is therefore part of the present model in the form of an anticipated condition. If attained, it becomes something that the agent can register as an actual feature of its situation.

The search for the value 9

This is an example of directed behavior with randomness inside it. The candidate values arrive randomly. The rule for continuing or stopping is fixed. The page adds a version with memory. The program could store unsuccessful outputs in an array outside the generator and supply that information to later calls. A small numerical example makes the effect precise. Suppose the available integers are 0 through 9, and each fresh independent call is equally likely to give any of them. The expected number of draws including the successful draw is ten. The chance of having found 9 by the tenth draw is about 65.13 percent. If the same ten values are instead tried in uniformly random order without repetition, 9 is certain to occur within ten draws, and its average position is 5.5. These figures are an illustration using a specified range. The page’s program supplies the stopping rule, and its proposed memory gives a way to change the search when the candidate set is known.

Perception, decision, and execution

PERCEPTION is the rendering of phenomena within an agent’s frame of reference. Karbytes gives it several inputs. Sensory hardware receives new data from the physical environment. The article gives that anticipation a particular role. An agent can imagine its immediate surroundings remaining stable long enough to consider an action. What the program counts and what it draws

The statistics are records with three fields. COLOR gives the exact hexadecimal string. FREQUENCY gives the number of copies of that string in the current array. PROBABILITY is that count divided by the total number of entries currently in the array. A color that is absent has no record. As fractions, the numbers for a nonempty array sum to one. JavaScript prints decimal approximations for fractions such as one third and one sixth. These are proportions of the current contents. Their interpretation as odds of the next draw depends on every position having the same chance of selection.

The JavaScript separates the work into small functions. It reads the selected menu values, builds the two arrays, formats their tables, maintains the statistics, and prints timestamps using Date.now. A temporary array C holds a copy of A during shuffling. The program repeatedly chooses an index across the full current length of C, transfers that entry to the end of B, and removes it from C. During the subsequent draws, the affected statistics record is decremented and deleted if its count reaches zero. A replacement increments an existing record or creates one. The program recalculates proportions after the relevant changes. A newly created statistics record is inserted using its palette position as an index into the shorter record list. That is why the displayed statistics can eventually appear in an order different from the original menus.

The code also checks the lengths and values of its working arrays and reports caught errors to the browser console. Some source comments describe ten colors or a much longer quantity menu. The executable palette contains five entries, and the menu builder produces the integers zero through ten in ascending order. I ran the published JavaScript with controlled random inputs and stand-ins for the page controls. Both modes produced the expected numbers of result blocks for an empty start, the small example configurations, and the maximum of fifty entries. With fifty, the without-replacement run ended at zero entries and the replacement run ended at fifty. I used the published screenshots to examine the visual presentation.

Two calls in the draw routine change the probability model described by the tutorial. The integer generator takes an upper bound T, multiplies a random fraction smaller than one by T, and rounds down. A positive T gives possible outputs from zero through T minus one. The shuffle supplies the full length of its temporary array. The later removal routine instead supplies the current length of B minus one. Whenever B has two or more entries, the last position is excluded. With a single entry, multiplication by zero gives index zero, so that sole entry can be drawn.

For a concrete case, consider B containing red followed by green. Each occupies half the array, and the statistics correctly report both proportions as 0.5. Every random input to the removal routine picks red from that particular ordered array. More generally, for a current array of length M greater than one, the next-draw calculation uses M minus one eligible positions. The eligible count for a color is its full count minus one if it occupies the last position, or its full count otherwise. Dividing that eligible count by M minus one gives the chance under an ideal uniform random input.

The replacement choice has the same upper-bound error. The palette has five entries and the routine supplies four as the exclusive upper bound. New entries can therefore be red, blue, violet, or yellow. Green can enter through the starting menus and survive subsequent draws, but its count can only stay the same or fall. There is also a short-lived consequence for every incoming entry. Since it is appended at the end, it is protected from the immediately following draw whenever B has at least two entries. A subsequent append moves it out of that protected position.

There is a subtle qualification in the without-replacement mode. Before the order of a uniformly shuffled B is observed, each initial entry has an equal chance of occupying any position. A selection rule that acts on positions independently of their colors can still produce an ordinary random ordering of the original population overall. Even reading a uniformly shuffled list strictly from top to bottom would do that. The discrepancy here appears when the displayed order of B is known. The interface shows that order, and the location of the last entry then changes the odds one can infer for the next selection. In replacement mode the palette restriction remains even if the current order is hidden.

How the work grows

Let T(N) be the number of calls in one recursive traversal, including the initial invocation. T(0) and T(1) are both 1. static_block_multiverse_model_of_reality

karbytes’s essay proposes that reality can be static as a whole and appear to grow from within. The whole is a timeless block multiverse containing every superposition of every phenomenon.
